title: DSA in Java: graphs, BFS/DFS and topological sort
seriesDescription: Hashing, windows, stacks, binary search, lists, trees, heaps and graphs with Java code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Java graph code: adjacency lists, grid DFS, Kahn's algorithm with ArrayDeque, cloning with a HashMap, and the identity-equality trap of int[] keys.
source: Oracle Java documentation (ArrayDeque, Collections.nCopies, arrays, StackOverflowError); LeetCode problem set; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview

questions.prompt: Write a Java method int numIslands(char[][] grid) counting the 4-directionally connected groups of '1' (land) in a grid of '1' and '0'. You may modify the grid.

checks.label: scans every cell with nested loops
starts a search only from land
marks visited cells by sinking the land or with a visited array
explores the four neighbours with a bounds check
increments a counter once per island

questions.explanation: Sinking visited land acts as the visited set, so no extra memory is needed beyond the recursion. For very large grids use an explicit ArrayDeque to avoid StackOverflowError.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method Node cloneGraph(Node node) that deep-copies a connected undirected graph (Node has int val and List<Node> neighbors, with a constructor Node(int val)). Use a HashMap from original to copy.

checks.label: returns null for a null input

questions.explanation: Register the copy in the map before recursing into the neighbours, otherwise a cycle recurses forever. A BFS version works the same way.

questions.prompt: Match each Java structure with its role in graph algorithms.

right.text: The BFS queue (and Kahn's ready queue)
Constant-time visited marks for vertices numbered 0..n-1
An adjacency list for sparse graphs
The frontier of Dijkstra's algorithm, ordered by distance
Original-to-copy lookup while cloning a graph

questions.explanation: Choosing the structure is half of a graph answer: array-backed marks for dense integer ids, hash maps when nodes are objects, and a priority queue when edges have weights.

questions.text: With Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>(), BFS enqueues with q.{1}(v) and dequeues with q.{2}(); it runs in O(V + E) on an adjacency list, and marks a node visited when it is {3} so it is never queued twice.
questions.explanation: offer adds at the tail and poll removes from the head. Marking at dequeue time lets the same node sit in the queue many times.

questions.prompt: An ArrayDeque<Integer> d receives d.offer(1), d.offer(2), d.offer(3), d.push(4), d.pollLast(), d.poll(), d.push(5) in that order. What does d.peekLast() return?
questions.explanation: After the offers the deque is [1, 2, 3]; push(4) gives [4, 1, 2, 3]; pollLast removes 3; poll removes 4, leaving [1, 2]; push(5) gives [5, 1, 2]. The last element is 2. I ran it to confirm.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A HashSet<int[]> used as a visited set for grid cells will not recognise a cell that was added before.
questions.reason: Java arrays use identity-based equals and hashCode, so two int[] with the same contents are different keys.

whys.a: Correct: contains(new int[]{1, 2}) is false even after add(new int[]{1, 2}); encode the cell as r * cols + c, a List<Integer> or a record instead.
whys.b: R is exactly the reason, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: I ran the example and contains returned false. This is a frequent source of infinite BFS loops in grid problems.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Kahn's algorithm with an ArrayDeque and adjacency lists runs in O(V + E).
questions.reason: ArrayDeque offer and poll take O(1) amortised time.

whys.a: R only covers the queue operations, not the edge relaxations that make the total V + E.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R explains only the queue cost; the bound also needs each vertex and edge to be handled once.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Each vertex is queued once (V queue operations) and each edge decrements one in-degree (E steps), giving O(V + E).

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: For vertices numbered 0..n-1, a HashSet<Integer> is a faster visited structure than a boolean[].
questions.reason: HashSet lookups take O(1) time on average.

whys.a: A is false, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: R is true but a boolean[] is faster still (direct indexing, no boxing or hashing), so A is false.

questions.explanation: Use a primitive array when ids are small integers; use a HashSet or HashMap only when nodes are objects or the id range is huge.

questions.prompt: Which Java statement builds a broken adjacency list in which every vertex shares the same inner list?

options.why: Correct: nCopies repeats one object reference n times, so adding an edge for one vertex appears for all.
This calls the constructor for each element, so the lists are independent.

options.text: A loop that calls adj.add(new ArrayList<>()) n times
options.why: Each iteration creates a fresh list, so this is the safe standard form.

options.text: new HashMap<Integer, List<Integer>>() filled with computeIfAbsent
options.why: computeIfAbsent creates a fresh list per key, so there is no sharing.

questions.explanation: I ran the nCopies version: after adding to vertex 0, printing three vertices gave [[1], [1], [1]]. Always create the inner lists in a loop.

questions.prompt: A recursive DFS over a path graph with 100,000 nodes can throw StackOverflowError on a default Java thread stack, so an explicit stack is safer for deep graphs.

options.why: Correct: each frame uses stack space and the default stack holds only some thousands to tens of thousands of frames.
The default stack is limited; very deep recursion does overflow.

questions.explanation: Convert deep DFS to an iterative version with ArrayDeque, or run it on a thread created with a larger stack size.

questions.prompt: A new int[n] used for in-degrees starts with every element equal to -1 in Java, so it has to be filled with zeros first.

options.why: Java does not choose -1 for you.
Correct: numeric arrays start at 0, which is exactly what a counter array needs.

questions.explanation: Boolean arrays start false and object arrays start null, so new boolean[n] is a ready visited array.
